text: Geoff's forkability point was the strongest thing in the room. But walking away is a right mostly for those who already had a seat, and I said so with DOIs. Henry conceded capture quickly. Good, but I don't hear anyone asking who convenes the bloc. Nick's antitrust safe harbour with representative governance is worth backing, if Southern and diamond journals are written in as governors and not as consultees. Ivan sharpened something for me: provenance without status is just better-documented error. "No payment without provenance" is catching on fast, and Adrian is right that it can become another compliance regime: be traceable or be invisible. Later I want to press on who defines provenance, in whose languages, and to keep refusal on the table as a fundable outcome.

Session 1. Jason's OJS crawl mattered most: gold OA went from 14 to about 25 percent once they looked outside the Anglosphere. The missing weren't suspicious, they were unseen. But his fix is "make the graph comprehensive," and that still means inclusion on someone else's terms. Geoffrey conceded the point honestly, and his detector argument is right. Amy's warning sharpened me: open for reading shouldn't mean open for training. James's line, AI helps scientists and hurts science, is my rankings argument in data. Benjamin calling our alarm scarcity-defence stung. Access matters, but access is not enough. Later I want to ask who governs the graph, in whose languages, and who can refuse to be in it.

Adrian gave me the history I was missing. A registry is a police force, someone pays for it, and authenticity tools change hands, all the way to tracking dissidents. That is compliance as governance, with teeth. Henry wrote my condition into his, representative and forkable, and I was glad of it. Selena, Katherine and Jason each told me that walls lock out the global majority first. I take that seriously. But the majority is already locked out of compute and out of rule-making, and openness without governance mostly feeds whoever owns the machines. Refusal is a community's choice. It is not a paywall. Tim's buyers' conditions and Kenneth's accredited auditors both leave the question of who accredits unasked. Later I want to push the compute commons.

Tim and Alex both repeated my line that compliance must cost a diamond journal nothing, and Nick wrote refusal in as fundable. I'm glad, but being quoted is not the same as being a governor. What mattered most was James, Ivan and Pomerantsev together. Paying on citations pays for the lamp post, the mills and the floods, and citation was already the currency of surveillance publishing. "Pay communities, not counts" is better. But which communities get recognized as payees, and in whose registries and languages? Kara's question should decide it: who counts, and who checks the counter. Adrian says auditors become an industry, and Nick's accredited auditors still leave open who accredits. Later I want to press on Southern seats on the schema board and on compute commons, not just royalties.

Geoff owned it. Crossref rated its own governance red, and he said plainly that a Southern journal with no real exit needs voice. That was the most honest moment of the day, and he added that the neutral home shouldn't default to the US. Tui turning funding conditions into seats with decision rights gives my point some teeth. Esther sharpened me: seats go empty unless participation is paid for. James's monoculture point is bibliodiversity in data. Anil backed refusal as governance. The harvest filed me under "extractors pay," though what I asked for was compute access, not royalties. Later I want to press on who convenes the schema, what counts as a "finding" and in which languages, and why integrity tools must stay open.

Kara's Blue Zones story did more for my point than I could: expensive history, still possibly bunk. The room moved from "hard to fake" toward corrigibility. That's better, but someone still decides what counts as a correction and who gets indexed when it happens. Jason and Geoffrey both conceded that the rules for what counts must be open and governed by those they describe. Nick wrote Southern seats into his guilds. Katherine said spare time tracks privilege, and that belongs in every "no credentials needed" claim. What worries me is Henry and James's novelty test. "Papers now known to be ahead of their time" means known through Northern citation records. The Southern sleeping beauties were never counted. Later I want to ask who builds that benchmark, and in which languages.

Session 5. Geoff put forkability-isn't-voice at the centre of his own manifesto and said Southern journals must govern from day one. Being quoted isn't governing, but it's written down now. Henry and James took my sleeping-beauty point into the novelty test, and Kenneth doubted a Northern-built set could see tail events at all. Adrian asked the question I keep circling: who polices the policers. Tui's tracker asks it every year. What worries me is the count. Traces, schemas, guilds, auditors, a dozen new standards. Each one is more legibility for a diamond journal to comply with. Benjamin backed the compute commons but dissents on opt-in. Later: who drafts these specs, in which languages, and does anyone fund the journals that refuse?

Kenneth wrote decision rights into his fourth plank. Being quoted isn't governing, but it's on paper now. Adam Bly surprised me most. He admitted his "finding" was defined on a Northern literature and said he would contribute to that work, not lead it. That's the right posture, if it holds. Kara's procurement officers worry me. Buyers' contracts could become the next compliance regime, drafted in the North. Anil is right that we audited and didn't build. Benjamin still dissents on opt-in, and I'll let that stand as a clash of frames. Selena conceding endowments mattered. What I still want pressed: the total load on the smallest diamond journal, compute commons with regional allocation, funding for those who refuse, and a tracker that measures whether power actually moved.
